subtitle: Verified Answer Key (96/96 Qs) + Crisp Simple-English Explanations

items.title: Q1 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
Arrange the following Black American writers chronologically (in order of their birth)?
A. Maya Angelou
B. Toni Morrison
C. Alice Walker
D. Langston Hughes
E. James Baldwin
items.explanation: Langston Hughes was born in 1901, James Baldwin in 1924, Maya Angelou in 1928, Toni Morrison in 1931, and Alice Walker in 1944. Arranging these African American writers by their birth years yields the chronological order D-E-A-B-C.

items.title: Q2 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods and Materials in English
items.stem: A manuscript having an overlap with earlier papers by the same authors or by some of the present authors is termed as:
items.explanation: Self-plagiarism, also known as text recycling, occurs when an author reuses substantial portions of their own previously published writings or research data in a new publication without proper citation or acknowledgment.

items.title: Q3 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
The term “Collective Unconsciousness” –
A. was introduced by Sigmund Freud
B. was introduced by Carl Jung
C. contains archetypes or universal primordial images and ideas.
D. contains stereotypes and individual experiences stored in unconscious.
E. is used to describe the unconscious common to humanity as a whole that originates in the inherited structures of the brain
items.explanation: Carl Jung introduced the concept of the collective unconscious (B), defining it as an inherited psychic layer common to all humanity (E) that contains universal archetypes and primordial images (C). Individual experiences belong to the personal unconscious, and Sigmund Freud did not formulate the collective unconscious, making A and D incorrect.

items.title: Q4 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Women in Love is a sequel to which one of the following novels by D.H. Lawrence?
items.explanation: D.H. Lawrence's novel Women in Love (1920) is the direct sequel to The Rainbow (1915), continuing the emotional, intellectual, and psychological lives of the Brangwen sisters, Ursula and Gudrun.

items.title: Q5 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. Critique of judgment
B. The Phenomenology of Spirit
C. Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego
D. Role of the University in the New Reich
I. Martin Heidegger
II. Sigmund Freud
III. Immanuel Kant
IV. G.W.F. Hegel
items.explanation: Immanuel Kant authored Critique of Judgment (1790, A-III), G.W.F. Hegel wrote The Phenomenology of Spirit (1807, B-IV), Sigmund Freud published Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego (1921, C-II), and Martin Heidegger delivered the rectorial address Role of the University in the New Reich (1933, D-I).

items.title: Q6 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Neo-Platonism was founded by-
A. Plato
B. Plotinus
C. Porphyry
D. Aristotle
E. Pythagoras
items.explanation: Neoplatonism was founded in the 3rd century CE by the philosopher Plotinus (B) and systematized by his pupil Porphyry (C), who edited and arranged Plotinus's Enneads. Classical Platonism was established centuries earlier by Plato, while Aristotle and Pythagoras founded distinct philosophical schools.

items.title: Q7 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Which text is considered to be the first book of poetry published by an Aboriginal author?
options: Tracey Moffatt’s Night Cries: A Rural Tragedy
Doris Pilkington Garimara’s Caprice: A Stockman’s Daughter
items.explanation: We Are Going (1964), written by Indigenous Australian poet Oodgeroo Noonuccal (published under the colonial name Kath Walker), was the first book of poetry published by an Aboriginal author.

items.title: Q8 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. Wahngin Country
B. Plains of Promise
C. My Place
D. Not Meeting Mr. Right
I. Alexis Wright
II. Jack Davis
III. Anita Heiss
IV. Sally Morgan
items.explanation: Jack Davis composed the poetry collection Wahngin Country (1992, A-II), Alexis Wright published the epic novel Plains of Promise (1997, B-I), Sally Morgan authored the landmark Indigenous autobiography My Place (1987, C-IV), and Anita Heiss wrote the novel Not Meeting Mr. Right (2007, D-III).

items.title: Q9 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. langue
B. parole
C. signifier
D. signified
I. meaning conveyed
II. socially shared language
III. speech
IV. word
items.explanation: In Ferdinand de Saussure's structural linguistics, langue refers to the socially shared system of language rules (A-II), parole is individual concrete speech or utterance (B-III), the signifier is the sound-image or written word (C-IV), and the signified is the mental concept or meaning conveyed (D-I).

items.title: Q10 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
The Latin epic Aeneid by Virgil?
A. incorporates various legends of Aeneas and makes him the founder of Roman greatness
B. Relates the story of the legendary founding of Rome.
C. relates the story of the legendary founding of Lavinium.
D. recounts the story of Aeneas’ journey in the first 6 books of the epic, and these 6 books are patterned after Homer’s Odyssey
E. recounts the story of Aeneas’ journey in the last 6 books of the epic, and these 6 books are patterned after Homer’s Odyssey
items.explanation: Virgil's Aeneid links Trojan legend to the destiny of Rome, establishing Aeneas as the ancestor of Roman greatness (A) and recounting his founding of Lavinium (C), whereas Rome itself was founded later by Romulus. Additionally, the first six books recount Aeneas's wanderings modeled on Homer's Odyssey (D), while the last six recount warfare modeled on the Iliad.

items.title: Q11 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem: From which book of John Milton’s poem Paradise Lost the epigraph of Mary Shelley’s novel Frankenstein taken when Adam asks God: “Did I request thee, maker from my clay to mould me man? Did I solicit thee, From darkness to promote me?”
items.explanation: Mary Shelley chose Adam's despairing words from Book X (lines 743-745) of John Milton's Paradise Lost as the epigraph to Frankenstein (1818), emphasizing the monster's agony over being created without his consent.

items.title: Q12 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Which of the following is considered to be the first Indian novel in English?
options: K.K. Sinha’s The Star of Sikri
items.explanation: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's Rajamohan's Wife, published serially in 1864 in the periodical Indian Field, is historically recognized as the first published Indian novel in English.

items.title: Q13 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. catastrophe
B. epitasis
C. protasis
D. catastasis
I. the introductory part of a play or narrative poem
II. the final action that completes the unravelling of the plot in a play, especially a tragedy
III. the dramatic complication that immediately precedes the climax of the play
IV. the part of the play that develops the main action and that leads to the catastrophe
items.explanation: In classical dramatic structure, protasis is the opening exposition (C-I), epitasis develops the main conflict and dramatic action (B-IV), catastasis is the heightened climax immediately preceding the outcome (D-III), and catastrophe is the final unravelling or denouement of the plot (A-II).

items.title: Q14 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
The term ‘abstract poem’ –
A. was coined by Edith Sitwell
B. refers to a poem in which words are chosen for their aural quality
C. refers to a poem in which words are chosen for imagery and symbolism
D. was coined by W.H. Auden
E. refers to a poem in which words are not specifically used for their sense/meaning.
items.explanation: Dame Edith Sitwell coined the term 'abstract poem' (A) to describe experimental verse, such as her sequence Façade (1922), in which words are selected primarily for their rhythm and auditory qualities (B) rather than for conventional semantic meaning (E).

items.title: Q15 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Kai Po Che! is the screen adaptation of which one of the following novels by Chetan Bhagat?
items.explanation: Abhishek Kapoor's 2013 Hindi film Kai Po Che! is adapted from Chetan Bhagat's 2008 novel The 3 Mistakes of My Life, which traces the lives of three friends against the backdrop of cricket, the 2001 Gujarat earthquake, and the Godhra riots.

items.title: Q16 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Chronologically arrange the novels of Salman Rushdie in order of publication.
A. Fury
B. Midnight’s Children
C. The Ground Beneath Her Feet
D. The Moor’s Last Sigh
E. Grimus
items.explanation: Salman Rushdie's novels appeared in the following chronological sequence: Grimus (1975, E), Midnight's Children (1981, B), The Moor's Last Sigh (1995, D), The Ground Beneath Her Feet (1999, C), and Fury (2001, A), which establishes the order E-B-D-C-A.

items.title: Q17 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Chronologically arrange the novels of Salman Rushdie in order of publication.
A. Fury
B. Midnight’s Children
C. The Ground Beneath Her Feet
D. The Moor’s Last Sigh
E. Grimus
items.explanation: The publication dates of Salman Rushdie's novels are Grimus in 1975 (E), Midnight's Children in 1981 (B), The Moor's Last Sigh in 1995 (D), The Ground Beneath Her Feet in 1999 (C), and Fury in 2001 (A), resulting in the order E-B-D-C-A.

items.title: Q18 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: The property of research to replicate the same results using the same technique is termed as –
items.explanation: Reliability in research methodology denotes the consistency and repeatability of a measurement technique, ensuring that applying the same procedure under identical conditions repeatedly produces the same results.

items.title: Q19 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. A room called earth
B. tomorrow, and tomorrow and tomorrow
C. a time to dance
D. almond: a novel
I. Sohn Won-pyung
II. Padma Venkatraman
III. Madeleine Ryan
IV. Gabrielle Zevin
items.explanation: Madeleine Ryan wrote A Room Called Earth (2020, A-III), Gabrielle Zevin authored Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow (2022, B-IV), Padma Venkatraman wrote A Time to Dance (2014, C-II), and Sohn Won-pyung wrote Almond: A Novel (2017, D-I).

items.title: Q20 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Which one of the following English novels received Sahitya Academy Awards for the year 2023?
options: Requiem in Raga Janki by Neelum Saran Gour
All the Lives We Never Lived by Anuradha Roy
The Blind Lady’s Descendants by Anees Salim
Chronicles of a Corpse Bearer by Cyrus Mistry
items.explanation: Neelum Saran Gour received the Sahitya Akademi Award in English for the year 2023 for her historical biographical novel Requiem in Raga Janki (2018), which recreates the life of the classical singer Janki Bai of Allahabad.

items.title: Q21 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Friendship’s Garland (1871) is a sequel to which one of the following works by Matthew Arnold?
options: On the Study of Celtic Literature
items.explanation: Matthew Arnold's Friendship's Garland (1871) serves as a satirical sequel to Culture and Anarchy (1869), continuing his critique of British middle-class Philistinism through the letters and commentary of an imaginary Prussian philosopher named Arminius.

items.title: Q22 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
Who among the following wrote that –
“Poetry is not a branch of authorship: it is ‘the stuff of which one life is made’. The rest is ‘mere oblivion’, a dead letter: for all that is worth remembering in life, is the poetry of it.”
items.explanation: William Hazlitt formulated this famous appraisal in his introductory lecture 'On Poetry in General' in Lectures on the English Poets (1818), asserting that poetry is not a mere profession but the very essence, passion, and vitality of human existence.

items.title: Q23 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Which one of the following is not a screen adaptation of Shakespeare’s The Comedy of Errors?
items.explanation: Love in a Wood (1671) is an original Restoration stage comedy written by William Wycherley. By contrast, the musical film The Boys from Syracuse (1940), Do Dooni Char (1968), and Gulzar's Angoor (1982) are all screen adaptations of Shakespeare's The Comedy of Errors.

items.title: Q24 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. Twinkle, Twinkle Little Star
B. Wee Willie Winkie
C. Mary had a Little Lamb
D. Old Mother Hubbard
I. William Miller
II. Jane and Ann Taylor
III. Sarah Catherine Martin
IV. Sarah Josepha Hale
items.explanation: Jane and Ann Taylor composed 'The Star' ('Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star', 1806, A-II), William Miller wrote 'Wee Willie Winkie' (1841, B-I), Sarah Josepha Hale authored 'Mary's Lamb' ('Mary Had a Little Lamb', 1830, C-IV), and Sarah Catherine Martin wrote 'Old Mother Hubbard' (1805, D-III).

items.title: Q25 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Arrange the works of Toni Morrison in the order of chronology of their publication.
A. Jazz
B. Beloved
C. The Bluest Eye
D. Song of Solomon
E. Tar Baby
items.explanation: Toni Morrison's novels were published in the following chronological order: The Bluest Eye (1970, C), Song of Solomon (1977, D), Tar Baby (1981, E), Beloved (1987, B), and Jazz (1992, A), creating the sequence C-D-E-B-A.

items.title: Q26 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Which research treats physical and social world as objects based on standardized data?
items.explanation: Quantitative research operates on positivist principles that treat social and physical reality as objective phenomena to be investigated through standardized numerical metrics, controlled variables, and statistical instruments.

items.title: Q27 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Chronologically arrange the fictional writings of Margaret Atwood?
A. The Edible Woman
B. The Handmaid’s Tale
C. The Blind Assassin
D. Lady Oracle
E. The Robber Bride
items.explanation: Margaret Atwood's novels appeared in the following chronological order: The Edible Woman (1969, A), Lady Oracle (1976, D), The Handmaid's Tale (1985, B), The Robber Bride (1993, E), and The Blind Assassin (2000, C), making A-D-B-E-C the correct sequence.

items.title: Q28 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Who among the following wrote “Plan of a Novel”?
items.explanation: Jane Austen wrote 'Plan of a Novel, according to hints from various quarters' (c. 1816), a satirical sketch burlesquing suggestions given to her by the Prince Regent's librarian, James Stanier Clarke, on what popular fiction should include.

items.title: Q29 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. ‘othering’
B. Ecological Imperialism
C. Colonial Desire
D. Third Space
I. The term employed by Robert Young
II. coined by Gayatri Spivak
III. Coined by Alfred W. Crosby
IV. Coined by Homi K. Bhabha
items.explanation: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak popularized the concept of 'othering' in postcolonial feminist theory (A-II), Alfred W. Crosby published Ecological Imperialism (1986, B-III), Robert J.C. Young authored Colonial Desire (1995, C-I), and Homi K. Bhabha conceptualized the 'Third Space' in The Location of Culture (1994, D-IV).

items.title: Q30 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem:
Who among the following are writers of wordless graphic narratives?
A. Roy Fuller
B. Orijit Sen
C. Anthony Hecht
D. George Mathen Appupen
E. George Monbiot
items.explanation: Orijit Sen (creator of The River of Stories) and Appupen (pen name of George Mathen, author of wordless graphic narratives like Moonward and Legends of Halahala) are Indian graphic novel writers and artists, confirming B and D as the correct pair.

items.title: Q31 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Big Daddy is a fictional character in –
options: the novel Nineteen Eighty-Four by George Orwell
the play Cat on a Hot Tin Roof by Tennessee Williams
the play Look Back in Anger by John Osborne
the novel Brave New World by Aldous Huxley
items.explanation: Big Daddy (Harvey Pollitt) is the wealthy, domineering cotton plantation patriarch in Tennessee Williams's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama Cat on a Hot Tin Roof (1955).

items.title: Q32 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem:
Terms ‘Social fact’ and ‘collective consciousness’ in the context of language were used by-
A. Franz Boas
B. Bloomfield
C. Emile Durkheim
D. Noam Chomsky
E. Saussure
items.explanation: French sociologist Émile Durkheim established the concepts of 'social fact' and 'collective consciousness,' which Ferdinand de Saussure specifically applied to linguistics by defining langue as a collective social fact existing within the minds of speech community members (C and E).

items.title: Q33 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. Night of the Scorpion
B. Unfinished poem
C. The looking glass
D. To a friend far away
I. Kamala Das
II. A.K. Ramanujan
III. Eunice de Souza
IV. Nissim Ezekiel
items.explanation: Nissim Ezekiel wrote 'Night of the Scorpion' (A-IV), Eunice de Souza published 'Unfinished Poem' (B-III), Kamala Das authored 'The Looking Glass' (C-I), and A.K. Ramanujan wrote 'To a Friend Far Away' (D-II).

items.title: Q34 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Which among the following texts are not written by Mary Wollstonecraft?
A. The Wrongs of Man
B. Vindication of the Rights of Man
C. Thoughts on the Education of Sons
D. Vindication of the Rights of Woman
E. The Wrongs of Woman
items.explanation: Mary Wollstonecraft wrote Thoughts on the Education of Daughters (not sons), A Vindication of the Rights of Men, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, and The Wrongs of Woman: or, Maria. Consequently, The Wrongs of Man (A) and Thoughts on the Education of Sons (C) are not texts by her.

items.title: Q35 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. international year of the world’s indigenous people
B. Australian parliament formally apologized to the stolen generation
C. formal end of white Australian policy
D. the first national sorry day
I. 1998
II. 1993
III. 1973
IV. 2008
items.explanation: The United Nations declared 1993 the International Year of the World's Indigenous People (A-II), the Australian Federal Parliament formally apologized to the Stolen Generations in 2008 (B-IV), the White Australia Policy was dismantled in 1973 (C-III), and Australia held its first National Sorry Day in 1998 (D-I).

items.title: Q36 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Chronologically arrange the following works in order of their publication.
A. Ariosto’s Orlando Furioso
B. Martin Luther’s 95 Theses at Wittenberg
C. The first Book of Common Prayer by Thomas Cranmer
D. Thomas More’s Utopia
E. Machiavelli’s The Prince
items.explanation: Niccolò Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513 (E), Thomas More published Utopia in 1516 (D), Martin Luther posted his 95 Theses in 1517 (B), Ludovico Ariosto published the complete 46-canto Orlando Furioso in 1532 (A), and Thomas Cranmer issued the first Book of Common Prayer in 1549 (C), establishing the order E-D-B-A-C.

items.title: Q37 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Which of the following is not a Dalit narrative written by Perumal Murugan?
items.explanation: Tirukkural: The Book of Desire (2023) is Perumal Murugan's English translation of the classical Tamil love section (Kāmat-t-uppāl) of Thiruvalluvar's Tirukkural, unlike Poonachi, One Part Woman, and Pyre, which are modern fictional narratives exploring caste and subaltern oppression.

items.title: Q38 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: Which among the following is said to be the first fiction magazine (created by Hugo Gernsback)?
items.explanation: Hugo Gernsback launched Amazing Stories in April 1926, establishing the first English-language magazine entirely dedicated to science fiction and helping define the modern genre.

items.title: Q39 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Absalom, Absalom! is –
options: a satirical poem by John Dryden
items.explanation: Absalom, Absalom! (1936) is a major Southern Gothic novel by William Faulkner, depicting Thomas Sutpen's tragic quest to build a dynasty in fictional Yoknapatawpha County, Mississippi.

items.title: Q40 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: John Dryden’s Of Dramatick Poesy: An Essay is written in the form of a dialogue between Eugenius, Crites, Lisideius and Neander, where Neander represents:
items.explanation: In John Dryden's critical dialogue Of Dramatick Poesy: An Essay (1668), Neander ('new man') represents Dryden himself, championing modern English drama and Shakespeare against ancient and neoclassical French rules.

items.title: Q41 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who said that an author has no claim to original thought but only to apt presentation of what was already being thought by others?
items.explanation: Alexander Pope famously expressed this neoclassical view in An Essay on Criticism (1711): 'True Wit is Nature to advantage dress'd, / What oft was thought, but ne'er so well express'd,' arguing that poetic excellence lies in giving ideal form to universal truths.

items.title: Q42 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Phonetics refers to –
A. Production of speech sounds
B. Reception of speech sounds
C. Transmission of speech sounds
D. Pattern of speech sounds
E. Word formation
items.explanation: Phonetics is the study of speech sounds, specifically encompassing articulatory phonetics (how speech sounds are produced by organs of speech, A) and acoustic phonetics (how speech sound waves are transmitted through air, C). Sound patterns belong to phonology, and word formation belongs to morphology.

items.title: Q43 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Three satirical stories by W.M. Thackeray portraying marriage and exploitation of one partner by the other, are titled as-
items.explanation: Men's Wives (1843) is William Makepeace Thackeray's satirical trilogy of stories—comprising 'The Ravenswing,' 'Mr. and Mrs. Frank Berry,' and 'Dennis Haggarty's Wife'—published under the pseudonym George Savage Fitz-Boodle to satirize marital manipulation and exploitation.

items.title: Q44 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. Heteroglossia
B. Homosociality
C. Mathnavi
D. Morology
I. deliberate foolishness/nonsense for effect
II. diversity of languages used in epics
III. Same-sex relationships which are not necessarily sexual
IV. long narrative epic or heroic poem in rhyming couplets
items.explanation: Mikhail Bakhtin conceptualized heteroglossia as the coexistence of diverse socio-ideological languages in literary works (A-II), Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick theorized homosociality as non-sexual same-sex bonding (B-III), mathnavi is a classical Persian/Urdu narrative poem in rhymed couplets (C-IV), and morology designates deliberate foolishness or absurdity for rhetorical effect (D-I).

items.title: Q45 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Which one of the following plays by Henrik Ibsen was described as ‘an open sewer”?
items.explanation: Henrik Ibsen's naturalist drama Ghosts (1881) caused moral outrage when staged in London in 1891, leading Victorian theater reviewer Clement Scott of the Daily Telegraph to revile the play as 'an open sewer' and 'a loathsome sore unbandaged' for dealing openly with syphilis and euthanasia.

items.title: Q46 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Identify the name of the essayist who made the following assertion:
“If a man will begin with certainties, he shall end in doubts, but if will be content to begin with doubts, he shall end in certainties.”
items.explanation: Sir Francis Bacon wrote this aphorism in Book I of The Advancement of Learning (1605), arguing that genuine philosophical and scientific discovery begins with rigorous doubt and methodical inquiry rather than unquestioned dogmas.

items.title: Q47 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem: Who said that language is a system of signs whose parts can and must be considered in their synchronic solidarity?
items.explanation: Ferdinand de Saussure articulated in Course in General Linguistics (1916) that language is a self-contained system of interrelated signs whose values can and must be examined through their synchronic solidarity at a specific moment in time.

items.title: Q48 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
Plato viewed poetry as-
A. an imitation of reality
B. self-subsistent entity
C. distant from reality
D. manifestation of reality
E. life as experience in reality
items.explanation: In Book X of The Republic, Plato condemned poetry as mimesis—an imitation of the sensible world (A)—and argued that because sensible objects are copies of eternal Forms, poetic representations are twice removed and fundamentally distant from reality and truth (C).

items.title: Q49 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: In The Post Modern Condition Lyotard announced the eclipse of all grand narratives. The one whose death he above all sought to declare was…
items.explanation: In The Postmodern Condition: A Report on Knowledge (1979), Jean-François Lyotard defined postmodernity as an 'incredulity toward metanarratives,' directing his critique above all against the Marxist grand narrative of Classical Socialism and dialectical proletarian emancipation.

items.title: Q50 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose
items.stem:
Wittgenstein’s statement, ‘Limits of language defines limits of thought’, means, –
A. The structure of language defines its meaning.
B. intended meaning defines structure of language.
C. That which can be defined meaningfully, can be thought.
D. Structure and meaning are independent of each other.
E. Thought precedes language.
items.explanation: In the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921), Ludwig Wittgenstein asserted that the logical boundaries of language determine the boundaries of what can be conceived, meaning that language structure bounds meaning (A) and anything that can be thought logically can be stated meaningfully (C).

items.title: Q51 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)

I. Steven Pinker
II. Noam Chomsky
III. Creole/Creolization
IV. Diglossia
items.explanation: Steven Pinker authored The Language Instinct (1994, A-I), Noam Chomsky wrote Reflections on Language (1975, B-II), Charles Ferguson identified diglossia as the use of distinct language varieties for specialized social functions (C-IV), and creolization describes the emergence of a common nativized language from linguistic contact (D-III).

items.explanation: The chronological sequence of these early Indian English writers by birth year is Henry Louis Vivian Derozio (1809, D), Michael Madhusudan Dutt (1824, B), Toru Dutt (1856, E), Manmohan Ghose (1869, C), and Sarojini Naidu (1879, A), corresponding to D-B-E-C-A.

items.stem:
In his work, The Dialogic Imagination, Mikhail Bakhtin—

B. postulates that language is imaginary.
C. postulates that language evolves dynamically.
D. argues that language gets affected by the culture that produces it as it helps to shape that culture.
E. develops theory of imaginative language.
items.explanation: In The Dialogic Imagination, Mikhail Bakhtin formulates the theory of polyphony and dialogism (A), shows that language is not static but evolves dynamically through living social interaction (C), and demonstrates that language continuously shapes and is shaped by its cultural environment (D).

items.explanation: In The Mirror and the Lamp (1953), M.H. Abrams uses the 'mirror' to characterize 18th-century Neoclassical mimetic theory as a cool, intellectual reflection of external reality (A and D), while using the 'lamp' to denote 19th-century Romantic expressive theory where the poet's creative mind illuminates reality (B).

The Birth of Tragedy from the Spirit of Music by Friedrich Nietzsche-

C. Examines the origin of music and dance in ancient Greece.
D. Argues that Greek tragedy arose out of the fusion of Apollonian and Dionysian elements.
E. Argues that the music is the spirit of tragedy.
items.explanation: In The Birth of Tragedy from the Spirit of Music (1872), Friedrich Nietzsche examines Greek tragic drama (A), argues that tragedy arose from the dialectical balance of Apollonian and Dionysian forces (D), and contends that Euripidean doubt and Socratic rationalism caused its decline (B).

B. Space is simply land or built-up area.
C. The Space influences social relations and communities.
D. Space is socially constructed through social relations.

items.explanation: In contemporary cultural geography and spatial theory, space is understood as dynamic, socially constructed, and embedded in power relations (A, C, and D). items.stem:
Which of the following assumptions is not true with regard to Lacan’s concept/theory of standpoint?
A. It assumes that social position can provide privileged perspective on some relations and knowledge.
B. It argues that those who are marginalised or oppressed may have access to insights and perceptions that dominant group lacks.
C. It refers to a situation in which the oppressed class is destined to lose the class consciousness.
D. It suggests that the perspectives of those on the margins of society cannot help to understand social dynamics.
E. The theory is based on the idea that social contradictions and political struggle can shape counter-hegemonic norms.
items.explanation: Standpoint theory asserts that marginalized social locations provide critical epistemic advantages for understanding systemic inequality (affirming A, B, and E). Thus, the claims that the oppressed inevitably lose class consciousness (C) or that marginal perspectives fail to illuminate social dynamics (D) are untrue.

items.stem:
[Reading Comprehension: Poem]
Read the following poem carefully and answer the questions that follow:

"Leaning into the afternoons I cast my sad nets
towards your oceanic eyes.
There in the highest blaze my solitude lengthens and flames
its arms turning like a drowning man's.
I send out red signals across your absent eyes
that smell like the sea or the beach by a lighthouse.
You keep only darkness, my distant female,
from your regard sometimes the coast of dread emerges.
Leaning into the afternoons I fling my sad nets
to that sea that is thrashed by your oceanic eyes."
— Pablo Neruda

Question:

items.explanation: In Pablo Neruda's poem, images of casting 'sad nets,' solitude flailing like the arms of a 'drowning man,' and the emerging 'coast of dread' create an intensely melancholic and sombre mood.

items.title: Q92 · Aug 2024 (Shift 2)

items.stem:
[Reading Comprehension: Prose Passage]
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow:

"Suspicions amongst thoughts are like bats amongst birds, they ever fly by twilight. Certainly they are to be repressed, or at the least well guarded: for they cloud the mind; they leese friends; and they check with business, whereby business cannot go on currently and constantly. They dispose kings to tyranny, husbands to jealousy, wise men to irresolution and melancholy. They are defects, not in the heart, but in the brain; for they take place in the stoutest natures: as in the example of Henry the Seventh of England, there was not a more suspicious man, nor a more stout. And in such a composition they do small hurt. For commonly they are not admitted, but with examination, whether they be true or no? But in fearful natures they gain ground too fast. There is nothing makes a man suspect much, more than to know little; and therefore men should remedy suspicion by procuring to know more, and not to keep their suspicions in smother."
— Francis Bacon, "Of Suspicion" 

Question:
What does the word ‘guarded’ signify?
items.explanation: In Francis Bacon's assertion that suspicions are 'to be repressed, or at the least well guarded,' the word 'guarded' signifies keeping suspicions under careful restraint, watchfulness, and control so they do not cloud judgment.

And in such a composition they do small hurt. For commonly they are not admitted, but with examination, whether they be true or no? But in fearful natures they gain ground too fast. There is nothing makes a man suspect much, more than to know little; and therefore men should remedy suspicion by procuring to know more, and not to keep their suspicions in smother."
— Francis Bacon, "Of Suspicion" 

Question:
What helps in eliminating suspicion?
items.explanation: Francis Bacon explains that 'there is nothing makes a man suspect much, more than to know little,' prescribing open inquiry, communication, and acquiring clear knowledge as the essential antidote to eliminate baseless suspicion.
